presentation: Purpose of urine ACR testing in diabetes
stem:
Priya, a 41-year-old shop manager, was found to have type 2 diabetes six months ago. At her first annual check with the practice nurse she is asked to bring an early-morning urine pot. She feels well, passes urine normally and asks why a urine sample is needed when her bladder is fine.

What is the main reason for this test?

options.A: To pick up early kidney damage from diabetes before it causes symptoms
options.B: To look for bacteria that could indicate a silent bladder infection
options.C: To check her glucose control instead of a blood test
options.D: To screen for blood in the urine from a bladder tumour
options.E: To confirm the diagnosis of diabetes made six months ago

correct_answer: A. To pick up early kidney damage from diabetes before it causes symptoms
why_correct: An early-morning urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio (ACR) detects albuminuria, which is the earliest sign of diabetic kidney disease and appears long before eGFR falls or symptoms develop. Finding it early allows blood pressure, glucose and renal-protective treatment (such as an ACE inhibitor or ARB) to be optimised. NICE recommends ACR at least annually in all adults with diabetes.
why_wrong: B. Routine screening for asymptomatic bacteriuria is not recommended outside pregnancy, and ACR does not detect infection. C. Urine glucose is an unreliable marker of control; HbA1c is used for monitoring. D. Haematuria is not what ACR measures, and she has no risk features for bladder cancer. E. Diabetes is diagnosed with blood tests such as HbA1c or plasma glucose, not urine.
pearl: Albuminuria is an independent marker of raised cardiovascular risk as well as of diabetic kidney disease.
thinking: Adult with diabetes at annual review ↓ No urinary symptoms ↓ Early-morning urine sample requested ↓ ACR measures albumin leak through the glomerulus ↓ Purpose is early detection of diabetic kidney disease
exam_trap: B, Looking for a silent bladder infection — a urine pot suggests a test for infection, but ACR measures albumin and asymptomatic bacteriuria is not screened for in non-pregnant adults.
takeaway: Annual urine ACR in diabetes is done to find diabetic kidney disease before it becomes symptomatic.

stem:
A 71-year-old retired builder with type 2 diabetes sees the practice nurse at his yearly review. He lives alone, wears work boots most days and says his feet look fine to him. Both feet have intact skin with no ulcers, calluses or deformity.

Which measure is most important to prevent foot complications in him?

options.A: Soaking his feet in hot water every evening to keep the skin soft
options.B: Using an over-the-counter corn plaster on any hard skin
options.C: A foot examination with risk assessment at least every year
options.D: Seeing a podiatrist only if an ulcer develops
options.E: Going barefoot at home to let the skin breathe

correct_answer: C. A foot examination with risk assessment at least every year
why_correct: NICE recommends that every adult with diabetes has their feet examined at least once a year, including testing for neuropathy with a 10 g monofilament, checking pulses and looking for deformity or skin changes. The result places him in a risk category that decides how often he is reviewed and whether he needs foot protection services. Prevention depends on finding risk before damage occurs, even when the feet look normal to the patient.
why_wrong: A. Hot soaks risk burns in a neuropathic foot and macerate the skin. B. Corn plasters contain acid that can ulcerate diabetic skin. D. Waiting for an ulcer misses the chance to prevent one. E. Walking barefoot exposes an insensate foot to unnoticed injury.
pearl: A diabetic foot problem with spreading infection, ischaemia or a new ulcer needs referral to the multidisciplinary foot care service within one working day.
thinking: Older man with diabetes ↓ Feet look normal but sensation may be reduced ↓ Ulcers start from unnoticed injury ↓ Annual examination stratifies risk ↓ Regular foot assessment is the key preventive step
exam_trap: D, Seeing a podiatrist only if an ulcer develops — it sounds sensible to involve specialists when needed, but foot care in diabetes is about prevention, and risk must be assessed before an ulcer appears.
takeaway: Every adult with diabetes needs at least annual foot risk assessment, even if the feet appear healthy.

stem:
A 47-year-old taxi driver with type 1 diabetes for 20 years tells his GP he wants to skip his eye screening appointment because his eyesight is perfect and he has just passed a driving eye test.

What is the most important reason to encourage him to attend?

options.A: Screening is mainly to look for cataract caused by high glucose
options.B: Screening is needed so his HbA1c can be checked less often
options.C: Sight-threatening retinopathy can develop while vision is still normal
options.D: Screening is the main way glaucoma is diagnosed in diabetes
options.E: Screening is mainly to measure his blood pressure effects on the eye

correct_answer: C. Sight-threatening retinopathy can develop while vision is still normal
why_correct: Diabetic retinopathy, including proliferative disease and maculopathy, can be advanced while visual acuity remains normal. Retinal photography finds these changes at a stage when laser or anti-VEGF treatment can prevent sight loss. Normal vision is therefore not reassurance, and he should keep attending the NHS Diabetic Eye Screening Programme.
why_wrong: A. Cataract is more common in diabetes but is not what the programme is designed to detect. B. Eye screening does not replace HbA1c or other annual checks. D. Glaucoma is detected by optometrists through pressure and field testing, not diabetic photographic screening. E. The programme grades diabetic retinopathy, not hypertensive changes.
pearl: Diabetic retinopathy is a leading cause of sight loss in working-age adults in the UK, and much of it is preventable through screening and timely treatment.
thinking: Long-standing type 1 diabetes ↓ Wants to skip screening because vision is good ↓ Retinopathy is silent until late ↓ Early treatment prevents blindness ↓ Explain that normal vision does not exclude retinopathy
exam_trap: A, Looking for cataract — cataract is linked with diabetes and affects vision, but the screening programme targets retinopathy, which can threaten sight without any symptoms.
takeaway: Normal eyesight does not exclude sight-threatening diabetic retinopathy, so screening must continue.

stem:
A 16-year-old girl with type 1 diabetes is brought to the emergency department with abdominal pain, vomiting and deep sighing breathing. For three days she has had fever, dysuria and loin pain, and she admits she reduced her insulin because she was not eating. She has ketonaemia and a metabolic acidosis.

Which factor is most likely to have triggered this episode?

options.A: Excess carbohydrate intake over the previous week
options.C: An episode of hypoglycaemia the night before
options.D: Starting the combined oral contraceptive pill

why_correct: Her fever, dysuria and loin pain point to pyelonephritis, and infection is one of the commonest triggers for DKA. Illness raises counter-regulatory hormones such as cortisol and adrenaline, increasing insulin requirements, and her reduction of insulin made the deficit worse. Treating DKA includes looking for and treating the precipitating cause.
why_wrong: A. Overeating raises glucose but does not usually cause ketoacidosis without insulin deficiency. B. Exercise tends to lower glucose and is not a typical trigger. C. Hypoglycaemia is the opposite problem and does not lead to DKA. D. The combined pill does not precipitate DKA.
pearl: Sick-day rules for type 1 diabetes: never stop insulin, check glucose and ketones more often, and seek help if ketones rise or vomiting persists.
thinking: Type 1 diabetes with ketoacidosis ↓ Fever, dysuria and loin pain ↓ Insulin reduced because not eating ↓ Infection raises insulin needs ↓ Infection is the precipitant
exam_trap: A, Excess carbohydrate intake — high glucose seems the obvious cause of a high-glucose emergency, but ketoacidosis comes from insulin deficiency, typically worsened by illness such as infection.
takeaway: Infection, often with missed or reduced insulin, is a common precipitant of DKA.

stem:
A 27-year-old man with type 1 diabetes is admitted to the medical assessment unit with DKA after a week of vomiting. His first venous gas shows a potassium of 5.8 mmol/L and his ECG is normal. The junior doctor asks whether this means he has too much potassium overall.

Which statement best describes his potassium status?

options.A: His serum level is a reliable guide to his total body potassium
options.B: He has a true potassium excess and needs calcium gluconate
options.C: His total body potassium is likely to be depleted despite the raised serum level
options.D: Starting insulin will push his serum potassium higher, so it should be delayed
options.E: He will not need potassium replacement during this admission

correct_answer: C. His total body potassium is likely to be depleted despite the raised serum level
why_correct: In DKA, insulin deficiency and acidosis shift potassium out of cells, so the serum level can be normal or high, while osmotic diuresis and vomiting have caused large losses. Total body potassium is therefore low. Once fixed-rate insulin starts, potassium moves back into cells and the serum level falls quickly, so it must be monitored closely and potassium added to fluids when the level drops into the normal range.
why_wrong: A. The serum level reflects the shift out of cells, not total stores. B. There is no true excess, and calcium gluconate is for hyperkalaemia with ECG changes or very high levels. D. Insulin lowers serum potassium; it is not delayed for this level. E. Most patients need potassium replacement once insulin is running.
pearl: In DKA, potassium is not added to the first litre of fluid if the serum level is high, but is added to later bags once it falls into the normal range, with close monitoring.
thinking: DKA with raised serum potassium ↓ Acidosis and insulin lack shift potassium out of cells ↓ Vomiting and osmotic diuresis cause losses ↓ Total stores are low ↓ Insulin will drop the serum level, so monitor and replace
exam_trap: B, A true potassium excess needing calcium gluconate — a raised value suggests hyperkalaemia, but in DKA it is a redistribution, the ECG is normal, and the level will fall with insulin.
takeaway: In DKA, total body potassium is depleted even when the serum potassium is normal or high.

presentation: Treating hypoglycaemia in a conscious patient
stem:
On a surgical ward, a 58-year-old woman with insulin-treated type 2 diabetes becomes sweaty, shaky and irritable before lunch. She is alert, talking in full sentences and can swallow normally. Her capillary glucose is low.

What is the most appropriate first step?

options.B: Insert a cannula and give 50% glucose intravenously
options.C: Give her a sandwich and recheck at the next meal
options.D: Omit her next insulin dose and observe
options.E: Give a fast-acting glucose drink or tablets and recheck the glucose shortly afterwards

correct_answer: E. Give a fast-acting glucose drink or tablets and recheck the glucose shortly afterwards
why_correct: She is conscious, cooperative and able to swallow, so oral fast-acting carbohydrate such as glucose tablets, juice or a glucose drink is the first-line treatment. The capillary glucose is rechecked after about 10 to 15 minutes and treatment repeated if still low. Once it has recovered, a longer-acting carbohydrate snack or her meal prevents recurrence.
why_wrong: A. Glucagon is for patients who cannot safely take oral treatment. B. Intravenous glucose is for those who are unconscious or cannot swallow, and 50% glucose damages veins. C. Starchy food is absorbed too slowly to be the first treatment. D. Omitting insulin does not treat the current episode and her dose should be reviewed rather than simply stopped.
pearl: Do not omit insulin entirely in type 1 diabetes after a hypo; review the dose instead, as stopping it risks DKA.
thinking: Symptoms of hypoglycaemia on the ward ↓ Alert and able to swallow ↓ Oral route is safe ↓ Fast-acting carbohydrate first ↓ Recheck after 10 to 15 minutes, then longer-acting snack
exam_trap: B, Intravenous glucose — it seems the quickest fix, but it is reserved for patients who cannot swallow, and a conscious patient should be treated orally.
takeaway: A conscious hypoglycaemic patient who can swallow should have oral fast-acting glucose, then a recheck.

stem:
A 22-year-old woman with newly diagnosed type 1 diabetes is in the emergency department with DKA. She has had her first bag of sodium chloride 0.9% and a fixed-rate intravenous insulin infusion is being prepared. A nurse asks what the insulin is mainly meant to achieve.

What is the best answer?

options.A: To correct her dehydration by making the kidneys retain water
options.B: To bring her blood glucose into the normal range within an hour
options.C: To switch off ketone production so the acidosis resolves
options.D: To lower her potassium as the main goal of treatment
options.E: To increase breakdown of liver glycogen

correct_answer: C. To switch off ketone production so the acidosis resolves
why_correct: The key problem in DKA is insulin deficiency driving uncontrolled lipolysis and ketone production, which causes the acidosis. A fixed-rate insulin infusion suppresses lipolysis and ketogenesis so ketones clear and the acidosis corrects, while also lowering glucose. Resolution is judged by falling ketones and rising bicarbonate, not by glucose alone.
why_wrong: A. Fluids, not insulin, correct the dehydration. B. Glucose should fall steadily; rapid normalisation is not the goal and risks cerebral oedema in young people. D. The fall in potassium is a side effect to monitor, not the aim. E. Insulin inhibits glycogen breakdown.
pearl: When glucose falls below about 14 mmol/L in DKA, 10% glucose is added alongside the saline so the fixed-rate insulin can continue clearing ketones.
thinking: DKA with fluids under way ↓ Underlying problem is insulin deficiency ↓ Lipolysis and ketogenesis drive acidosis ↓ Insulin suppresses ketone production ↓ Aim is clearing ketones and correcting acidosis
exam_trap: B, Normalising glucose within an hour — high glucose is the striking number, but the danger in DKA is the ketoacidosis, and glucose should fall gradually.
takeaway: Insulin in DKA is given chiefly to stop ketogenesis and correct the acidosis.

stem:
A 34-year-old woman with vitiligo sees her GP with three months of tiredness, poor appetite, weight loss and light-headedness when she gets up. Her partner comments that she looks tanned despite a cold winter. Her lying and standing blood pressure shows a postural drop.

Which electrolyte result is most typical of her likely condition?

options.D: High serum calcium as the main finding
options.E: Low serum phosphate as the main finding

why_correct: Vitiligo, hyperpigmentation, weight loss, fatigue and postural hypotension suggest autoimmune primary adrenal insufficiency (Addison's disease). Loss of aldosterone causes renal sodium loss, and cortisol deficiency impairs free-water excretion, so hyponatraemia is the commonest electrolyte abnormality, often with hyperkalaemia. She needs urgent morning cortisol and ACTH testing.
why_wrong: B. Sodium is lost, not retained, in aldosterone deficiency. C. Hypokalaemic alkalosis suggests mineralocorticoid excess, the opposite of Addison's. D. Mild hypercalcaemia can occur but is neither common nor defining. E. Phosphate is not a characteristic abnormality.
pearl: Hyperpigmentation occurs in primary but not secondary adrenal insufficiency, because it is driven by high ACTH levels.
thinking: Fatigue, weight loss and postural dizziness ↓ Pigmentation and vitiligo ↓ Points to primary adrenal insufficiency ↓ Aldosterone and cortisol deficiency ↓ Hyponatraemia is typical
exam_trap: C, Low potassium with alkalosis — electrolyte disturbances in adrenal disease are easy to mix up, but this is the pattern of aldosterone excess, whereas Addison's causes low sodium and high potassium.
takeaway: Hyponatraemia, often with hyperkalaemia, is the typical electrolyte picture in Addison's disease.

stem:
A 61-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes for 25 years tells her GP that she nearly faints when she gets out of bed, feels full after small meals and has noticed she no longer sweats on her legs while her face sweats heavily at meals. Her blood pressure falls significantly on standing.

Which complication of diabetes best explains her symptoms?
why_correct: Postural hypotension, early satiety from gastroparesis and abnormal sweating (loss in the legs with gustatory facial sweating) together reflect damage to the autonomic nerves supplying the cardiovascular system, gut and sweat glands. This is diabetic autonomic neuropathy, which tends to occur after many years of diabetes alongside other microvascular complications.
why_wrong: A. Uraemia causes nausea and fatigue but not this combination of postural and sweating changes. B. Peripheral arterial disease causes claudication and ischaemic feet. C. Retinopathy affects vision only. E. Distal sensory neuropathy causes numbness and pain in the feet, not postural hypotension or sweating changes.
pearl: Cardiac autonomic neuropathy can cause a fixed resting tachycardia and silent myocardial ischaemia.
thinking: Long-standing diabetes ↓ Postural hypotension ↓ Early satiety ↓ Abnormal sweating pattern ↓ Multiple autonomic systems involved, so autonomic neuropathy
exam_trap: E, Distal sensory polyneuropathy — it is the commonest diabetic neuropathy, but it affects sensation in the feet and does not explain postural hypotension, gut or sweating symptoms.
takeaway: Postural hypotension, gut dysmotility and sweating changes in diabetes point to autonomic neuropathy.

stem:
A 45-year-old delivery van driver with insulin-treated type 2 diabetes tells his GP that twice in the last month he has had to pull over because he felt shaky and confused at the wheel, and his meter read low. He wants to keep working.

What is the most appropriate advice?

options.A: Stop driving now, explain his legal duty to follow DVLA rules on notification, and arrange an urgent review of his diabetes treatment
options.B: Continue driving but eat a snack every hour while on the road
options.C: Increase his insulin dose to improve his overall control
options.D: Continue driving as long as he can feel the warning symptoms
options.E: Stop checking his glucose before driving to reduce worry

correct_answer: A. Stop driving now, explain his legal duty to follow DVLA rules on notification, and arrange an urgent review of his diabetes treatment
why_correct: Hypoglycaemia at the wheel impairs judgement and reaction time and puts him and others at risk. He should stop driving until his hypoglycaemia is controlled, and it is his legal responsibility to inform the DVLA according to its rules for drivers on insulin. His insulin and lifestyle also need urgent review to find the cause of the episodes.
why_wrong: B. Snacking does not make driving safe when hypoglycaemia keeps occurring. C. Increasing insulin would make hypoglycaemia more frequent. D. Warning symptoms are not a safeguard when he is already becoming confused at the wheel. E. Drivers on insulin are required to check glucose before and during long journeys.
pearl: Drivers on insulin should check glucose no more than 2 hours before driving and every 2 hours on long journeys, and should not drive if the reading is below 5 mmol/L without eating first.
thinking: Insulin-treated diabetes ↓ Repeated hypoglycaemia while driving ↓ Danger to himself and the public ↓ Legal duty to follow DVLA rules ↓ Stop driving and review treatment
exam_trap: D, Continue driving while he can feel the warning symptoms — awareness of symptoms seems protective, but he has already become confused at the wheel, so continuing is unsafe.
takeaway: Hypoglycaemia while driving means stopping driving, following DVLA rules and reviewing treatment.

stem:
A 69-year-old woman with metastatic breast cancer is admitted with drowsiness, vomiting and constipation. Her corrected calcium is very high. Before starting intravenous fluids, an ECG is recorded.

Which ECG finding is most characteristic of this electrolyte disturbance?

options.C: Delta waves with a short PR interval
options.D: Saddle-shaped ST elevation in all leads
options.E: Peaked T waves with absent P waves

why_correct: Raised extracellular calcium speeds ventricular repolarisation, shortening the ST segment and therefore the QT interval. Severe hypercalcaemia, often from bone metastases in breast cancer, can also cause bradycardia and arrhythmias, so the ECG should be monitored during treatment with intravenous fluids and bisphosphonates.
why_wrong: A. A long QT interval is seen with low, not high, calcium. C. Delta waves indicate an accessory pathway such as Wolff-Parkinson-White. D. Widespread saddle-shaped ST elevation suggests pericarditis. E. Peaked T waves with loss of P waves are features of hyperkalaemia.
pearl: Hypocalcaemia lengthens the QT interval, while hypercalcaemia shortens it.
thinking: Malignancy with drowsiness, vomiting and constipation ↓ Severe hypercalcaemia ↓ Calcium speeds repolarisation ↓ ST segment and QT shorten ↓ Short QT interval
exam_trap: A, Lengthened QT interval — QT prolongation is linked to many electrolyte disorders, but it occurs with hypocalcaemia, whereas hypercalcaemia shortens the QT.
takeaway: Hypercalcaemia characteristically shortens the QT interval.

stem:
A 32-year-old man with schizophrenia living in supported accommodation is brought to the GP by staff who say he drinks from the tap constantly, often many litres a day. He has had two admissions with low sodium in the past year, each improving quickly once his intake was supervised. His glucose and kidney function are normal.

Which diagnosis best explains his recurrent hyponatraemia?
why_correct: Compulsive excessive water drinking, often seen in people with psychiatric illness, can exceed the kidneys' capacity to excrete free water and cause dilutional hyponatraemia. The urine is maximally dilute, and sodium recovers once intake is restricted, as happened during his admissions.
why_wrong: A. Diabetes insipidus causes loss of water with high or high-normal sodium, not hyponatraemia. B. Phaeochromocytoma causes episodic hypertension and sweating. C. Hyperparathyroidism causes hypercalcaemia and thirst but not low sodium. E. Conn's syndrome causes hypertension, hypokalaemia and a high-normal sodium.
pearl: In primary polydipsia the urine osmolality is very low, unlike SIADH where it is inappropriately high.
thinking: Compulsive drinking of large volumes ↓ Psychiatric illness ↓ Recurrent low sodium ↓ Corrects with restricted intake ↓ Primary polydipsia
exam_trap: A, Cranial diabetes insipidus — drinking large volumes suggests diabetes insipidus, but DI loses water and raises sodium, whereas excess intake dilutes it.
takeaway: Excessive water intake in primary polydipsia can cause recurrent dilutional hyponatraemia.
notes: Reviewer fix: stem wording: 'often more than several litres a day' -> 'often many litres a day'

presentation: Hypothyroidism as a cause of hyponatraemia
stem:
An 80-year-old care home resident is admitted with increasing drowsiness. Staff report that over the last year she has become slow, puffy-faced, constipated and always wants a blanket. She is not on diuretics. Bloods show a low sodium, a markedly raised TSH and low free T4, with normal cortisol.

Which condition is the most likely contributor to her low sodium?
why_correct: Her slowness, facial puffiness, constipation, cold intolerance and drowsiness with a high TSH and low free T4 indicate severe primary hypothyroidism. Severe hypothyroidism reduces cardiac output and glomerular filtration and impairs free-water excretion, causing hyponatraemia. Thyroid function is part of the standard work-up of hyponatraemia for this reason, and her drowsiness raises concern for myxoedema coma.
why_wrong: A. Conn's syndrome causes hypertension, hypokalaemia and a normal or high sodium. B. Thyrotoxicosis gives a suppressed TSH and does not cause hyponatraemia. C. Cushing's syndrome is excluded clinically and tends not to cause low sodium. E. Acromegaly causes coarse features and soft tissue growth but not this thyroid pattern.
pearl: Before diagnosing SIADH, hypothyroidism and adrenal insufficiency must be excluded, as both can mimic it.
thinking: Elderly woman with slowing, cold intolerance and constipation ↓ High TSH with low free T4 ↓ Severe primary hypothyroidism ↓ Impaired free-water excretion ↓ Hypothyroidism contributes to the hyponatraemia
exam_trap: B, Thyrotoxicosis — thyroid disease is clearly involved, but a high TSH with low free T4 indicates an underactive gland, and it is hypothyroidism that lowers sodium.
takeaway: Severe hypothyroidism is a recognised cause of hyponatraemia and should be checked in its work-up.

stem:
Ten days after her GP started bendroflumethiazide for hypertension, a 77-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department by her daughter because she is vomiting, muddled and has a headache. Her serum sodium is 116 mmol/L.

Which complication poses the most immediate threat to her?

options.C: Renal stones from altered calcium handling
options.D: Brain swelling leading to seizures or reduced consciousness

correct_answer: D. Brain swelling leading to seizures or reduced consciousness
why_correct: A sharp fall in sodium makes plasma hypotonic relative to brain cells, so water moves into the brain and causes cerebral oedema. Headache, vomiting and confusion are warning features that can progress to seizures, coma and herniation. This needs urgent senior management, with hypertonic saline considered for severe symptoms and close monitoring of the rate of correction.
why_wrong: A. Thiazides can raise glucose modestly but this is not an immediate threat. B. Raised urate is a recognised side effect but not life-threatening here. C. Thiazides actually reduce urinary calcium and stone risk. E. Haemoconcentration is not the main danger.
pearl: Thiazides are a common cause of hyponatraemia in older women, often within weeks of starting.
thinking: Recently started thiazide ↓ Profound hyponatraemia ↓ Vomiting, headache and confusion ↓ Water shifts into brain cells ↓ Cerebral oedema with seizures is the immediate threat
exam_trap: A, Thiazide-induced hyperglycaemia — it is a well-known thiazide effect, but it is minor compared with the life-threatening brain swelling from severe hyponatraemia.
takeaway: Symptomatic severe hyponatraemia threatens cerebral oedema, seizures and death.

stem:
A 64-year-old man is admitted with confusion two weeks after a severe pneumonia. His sodium is 119 mmol/L and his plasma osmolality is low. He has moist mucous membranes, no oedema, normal blood pressure and takes no diuretics. Thyroid function and cortisol are normal.

Which result would most support SIADH?

options.A: Urine osmolality higher than would be expected for his plasma osmolality
options.E: Plasma osmolality above the normal range

correct_answer: A. Urine osmolality higher than would be expected for his plasma osmolality
why_correct: In SIADH, ADH is secreted despite low plasma osmolality, so the kidneys keep reabsorbing water and the urine is inappropriately concentrated (urine osmolality above 100 mOsm/kg). Together with euvolaemia, a urine sodium usually above 30 mmol/L, no diuretics and normal thyroid and adrenal function, this supports the diagnosis. Pneumonia is a recognised cause.
why_wrong: B. A low urine sodium suggests low effective volume, such as dehydration or heart failure. C. Oedema points to a hypervolaemic cause. D. Marked hyperglycaemia causes a translocational hyponatraemia with normal or high osmolality. E. SIADH causes a low, not high, plasma osmolality.
pearl: SIADH is a diagnosis of exclusion; thyroid and adrenal function must be normal before it is made.
thinking: Hyponatraemia with low plasma osmolality ↓ Clinically euvolaemic, no diuretics ↓ Thyroid and cortisol normal ↓ ADH active despite hypotonicity ↓ Inappropriately concentrated urine supports SIADH
exam_trap: B, Urine sodium below 20 mmol/L — urine sodium is part of the work-up, but a low value points to volume depletion, whereas SIADH typically shows a raised urine sodium.
takeaway: In SIADH the urine is inappropriately concentrated despite a low plasma osmolality.

stem:
A 59-year-old woman with long-standing alcohol misuse is found to have a sodium of 108 mmol/L after weeks of poor eating. She is treated, and her sodium rises by 18 mmol/L in the first day. Three days later she develops slurred speech, difficulty swallowing and weakness of all four limbs.

Which complication has most likely occurred?
why_correct: Rapid correction of chronic hyponatraemia shrinks brain cells that had adapted to hypotonicity, damaging myelin, especially in the pons. The typical picture is a delay of a few days followed by dysarthria, dysphagia and quadriparesis, sometimes progressing to a locked-in state. Alcohol misuse and malnutrition increase the risk, so correction must be kept within safe limits.
why_wrong: A. Wernicke's causes confusion, ophthalmoplegia and ataxia, not quadriparesis after sodium correction. B. Cerebral oedema results from a fall in sodium, not from rapid correction. C. A stroke would be sudden in onset and would not explain a delayed, symmetrical bulbar and four-limb deficit following over-correction. D. Subarachnoid haemorrhage presents with sudden severe headache.
pearl: Over-correction of chronic hyponatraemia can be reversed by giving free water or desmopressin under specialist guidance.
thinking: Chronic profound hyponatraemia ↓ High-risk patient with alcohol misuse and poor nutrition ↓ Sodium corrected too quickly ↓ Delayed dysarthria, dysphagia and quadriparesis ↓ Osmotic demyelination syndrome
exam_trap: B, Cerebral oedema with herniation — this is the danger of untreated low sodium, but here the sodium was raised too quickly, which causes demyelination instead.
takeaway: Over-rapid correction of chronic hyponatraemia can cause osmotic demyelination syndrome.
notes: Reviewer fix: why_wrong C (stroke) given a real discriminating reason instead of a vague timing remark

stem:
A 42-year-old man with autoimmune Addison's disease asks the endocrinology registrar why he must take fludrocortisone as well as hydrocortisone. When he was first diagnosed he had a low blood pressure and a raised serum potassium.

Deficiency of which hormone was mainly responsible for his raised potassium?
why_correct: Aldosterone acts on the distal nephron to reabsorb sodium and secrete potassium. In primary adrenal insufficiency the adrenal cortex is destroyed, so aldosterone is lost and potassium is retained, causing hyperkalaemia. Fludrocortisone replaces this mineralocorticoid effect.
why_wrong: A. Cortisol deficiency contributes to hypotension and hypoglycaemia but is not the main cause of raised potassium. B. Thyroxine does not regulate renal potassium excretion. C. Growth hormone has no important role in potassium balance. E. ADH affects water handling and sodium concentration, not potassium.
pearl: Secondary adrenal insufficiency (pituitary cause) spares aldosterone, so hyperkalaemia is not a feature.
thinking: Primary adrenal insufficiency ↓ Adrenal cortex destroyed ↓ Loss of aldosterone ↓ Kidney cannot excrete potassium ↓ Hyperkalaemia, treated with fludrocortisone
exam_trap: A, Cortisol — it is the hormone most associated with Addison's disease, but potassium excretion is controlled by aldosterone.
takeaway: Aldosterone deficiency causes the hyperkalaemia of primary adrenal insufficiency.

stem:
While travelling abroad, a 55-year-old teacher left her medicines bag behind and has taken none of her twice-daily hydrocortisone or her fludrocortisone for four days. She takes these for autoimmune adrenal failure diagnosed years ago. On return she is taken by ambulance to A&E with cramping abdominal pain, retching and being too weak to stand. She is cold, clammy and hypotensive. Her chemistry panel shows sodium below and potassium above the reference range.

Which diagnosis is most likely?
why_correct: Stopping glucocorticoid and mineralocorticoid replacement in Addison's disease leaves her without cortisol or aldosterone, producing an adrenal crisis with vomiting, abdominal pain, hypotension, hyponatraemia and hyperkalaemia. This is a medical emergency needing immediate intravenous or intramuscular hydrocortisone and fluid resuscitation.
why_wrong: A. SIADH causes hyponatraemia with euvolaemia but not hyperkalaemia or shock. B. Conn's syndrome causes hypertension and hypokalaemia. C. Thyroid storm presents with fever, tachycardia and agitation. D. DKA needs raised glucose and ketones and does not follow stopping steroids.
pearl: Patients on steroid replacement should carry a steroid emergency card and an emergency hydrocortisone injection kit.
thinking: Known Addison's disease ↓ Ran out of replacement steroids ↓ Vomiting, weakness and hypotension ↓ Low sodium with high potassium ↓ Acute adrenal insufficiency
exam_trap: A, SIADH — hyponatraemia with vomiting may suggest it, but SIADH does not cause hyperkalaemia or hypotension, and the stopped steroids point to adrenal crisis.
takeaway: Stopping steroid replacement in Addison's disease can precipitate adrenal crisis.
notes: Reviewer fix: stem: colloquial 'crampy tummy pain' -> 'cramping abdominal pain'

stem:
A 70-year-old man with a known small-cell lung cancer has chronic mild hyponatraemia found on routine bloods before chemotherapy. He has no symptoms, is euvolaemic and his work-up is consistent with SIADH.

Which treatment approach is most appropriate first?

options.A: Encourage him to drink at least three litres a day
options.D: Give a rapid infusion of hypertonic saline
options.E: Start a loop diuretic as monotherapy

why_correct: In SIADH the kidneys cannot excrete free water, so reducing intake is the logical first step for asymptomatic chronic hyponatraemia. Fluid restriction allows the sodium to rise slowly. Treating the underlying cause is also important, and drugs such as tolvaptan are considered only by specialists if restriction fails.
why_wrong: A. Extra water worsens dilutional hyponatraemia. B. Potassium does not correct SIADH. D. Hypertonic saline is reserved for severe symptoms and must not be given rapidly in chronic hyponatraemia. E. A loop diuretic alone without salt intake is not first-line and can worsen sodium loss.
pearl: Fluid restriction is unlikely to work when the urine osmolality is very high or urine sodium plus potassium exceeds plasma sodium.
thinking: Small-cell lung cancer ↓ Chronic mild euvolaemic hyponatraemia ↓ SIADH with free-water retention ↓ Asymptomatic, so no urgent correction ↓ Fluid restriction first
exam_trap: D, Hypertonic saline — it raises sodium, but it is for severe symptoms, and rapid correction of chronic hyponatraemia risks osmotic demyelination.
takeaway: Fluid restriction is first-line for asymptomatic chronic hyponatraemia due to SIADH.

stem:
An 84-year-old man from a care home is sent to the emergency department because he has become newly confused and unsteady over two days. Routine bloods show a very low sodium. His carers mention he has early dementia.

What is the most appropriate approach?

options.A: Attribute the confusion to dementia and arrange discharge
options.B: Repeat the sodium in one week before deciding
options.C: Urgently assess the severity of symptoms, fluid status and likely cause, with senior input
options.D: Encourage him to drink more water
options.E: Give hypertonic saline to bring the sodium back to normal within 24 hours

correct_answer: C. Urgently assess the severity of symptoms, fluid status and likely cause, with senior input
why_correct: New confusion with a very low sodium suggests symptomatic hyponatraemia, which can progress to seizures and coma from cerebral oedema. He needs urgent assessment of symptom severity, volume status, medications and possible causes, with senior involvement to plan treatment. Correction must be controlled, as raising sodium too quickly risks osmotic demyelination.
why_wrong: A. Acute confusion should not be blamed on dementia without excluding a reversible cause. B. Waiting a week risks deterioration. D. Free water worsens most causes of hyponatraemia. E. Normalising sodium within 24 hours is far too fast and risks osmotic demyelination.
pearl: Drugs such as thiazides, SSRIs, carbamazepine and PPIs are frequent causes of hyponatraemia in older people.
thinking: Older man with new confusion ↓ Very low sodium ↓ Symptomatic hyponatraemia is dangerous ↓ Need severity, volume status and cause ↓ Urgent assessment with controlled correction
exam_trap: E, Hypertonic saline to normalise sodium within 24 hours — urgent treatment seems right, but full correction this fast can cause osmotic demyelination.
takeaway: Symptomatic severe hyponatraemia needs urgent assessment and carefully controlled correction.

stem:
A 57-year-old woman sees her GP with months of tiredness, low mood, thirst, passing more urine and constipation. She had a kidney stone last year. Her bloods show a raised calcium, low phosphate and a parathyroid hormone level that is high.

Which diagnosis is most likely?
why_correct: Raised calcium with an inappropriately high parathyroid hormone and low phosphate indicates primary hyperparathyroidism, most often from a parathyroid adenoma. Symptoms such as thirst, polyuria, constipation, low mood and kidney stones are classic features of hypercalcaemia. It is the commonest cause of hypercalcaemia in the community.
why_wrong: B. Hypoparathyroidism causes low calcium. C. Diabetes insipidus causes thirst and polyuria but does not raise calcium or PTH. D. Hypothyroidism causes constipation and tiredness but not hypercalcaemia. E. Secondary hyperaldosteronism affects sodium and potassium, not calcium.
pearl: Malignancy is the commonest cause of hypercalcaemia in hospital, whereas primary hyperparathyroidism is the commonest in primary care.
thinking: Thirst, polyuria and constipation ↓ Previous kidney stone ↓ High calcium with low phosphate ↓ PTH high rather than suppressed ↓ Primary hyperparathyroidism
exam_trap: C, Cranial diabetes insipidus — thirst and polyuria fit, but DI does not cause hypercalcaemia or stones, and the high PTH points to the parathyroid.
takeaway: High calcium with a raised PTH points to primary hyperparathyroidism.

stem:
A 52-year-old man with a high stoma output after bowel resection is reviewed on the surgical ward. He has developed fine twitching of his hands and painful calf spasms, and his serum magnesium has fallen well below normal. The nurse asks what serious problem this deficiency could lead to if it is not corrected.

Which complication is most important to anticipate?

options.A: Ventricular arrhythmias, including torsades de pointes
options.B: Fluid accumulation in the peritoneal cavity
options.C: A rise in red cell mass

correct_answer: A. Ventricular arrhythmias, including torsades de pointes
why_correct: Magnesium is needed to stabilise cardiac and neuromuscular membranes, so a significant deficiency increases excitability. Clinically this shows as tremor, cramps and tetany, and in the heart it can cause atrial and ventricular arrhythmias, notably torsades de pointes. Ongoing gut losses from a high output stoma are a classic cause, so magnesium should be replaced and an ECG checked.
why_wrong: B. Ascites relates to liver disease, heart failure or malignancy, not low magnesium. C. Polycythaemia has no link to magnesium deficiency. D. Low magnesium impairs parathyroid hormone release and action, causing hypocalcaemia rather than hypercalcaemia. E. Cataract is a chronic lens change and not a recognised consequence of hypomagnesaemia.
pearl: Hypokalaemia and hypocalcaemia often fail to correct until coexisting hypomagnesaemia is treated.
thinking: High output stoma causing gut magnesium loss ↓ Tremor and cramps show neuromuscular irritability ↓ Magnesium also stabilises cardiac membranes ↓ Deficiency predisposes to arrhythmias such as torsades ↓ Replace magnesium and check the ECG
exam_trap: D, Marked hypercalcaemia — calcium and magnesium are often linked in the mind, but low magnesium suppresses parathyroid hormone and causes hypocalcaemia.
takeaway: Significant hypomagnesaemia can provoke dangerous cardiac arrhythmias and should be corrected promptly.

stem:
A 63-year-old woman being treated for breast cancer tells her oncology nurse that she has felt muddled and very tired over the past fortnight. A blood test shows a markedly raised adjusted calcium. She asks which other symptom she might notice because of this result.

Which symptom is most consistent with her abnormality?

options.A: Sensitivity of the eyes to light

correct_answer: E. Passing large volumes of urine
why_correct: High calcium interferes with the action of antidiuretic hormone in the renal collecting ducts, producing a nephrogenic diabetes insipidus picture. This causes polyuria and compensatory thirst, which can lead to dehydration and further worsening of the calcium. Together with confusion and fatigue, this fits hypercalcaemia of malignancy in this woman.
why_wrong: A. Photophobia suggests meningism or migraine. B. Stridor reflects upper airway narrowing and is not a feature of a high calcium. C. Rhinorrhoea is not related to calcium levels. D. Haemoptysis may occur with lung disease but is not caused by hypercalcaemia itself.
pearl: Initial treatment of significant hypercalcaemia is intravenous fluid rehydration, followed by an intravenous bisphosphonate once rehydrated.
thinking: Known malignancy with confusion and fatigue ↓ Markedly raised calcium ↓ Calcium blunts renal response to antidiuretic hormone ↓ Urine cannot be concentrated ↓ Polyuria and thirst follow
exam_trap: D, Coughing up blood — a cancer patient may have lung metastases, but haemoptysis is caused by the lesion, not by the raised calcium.
takeaway: Hypercalcaemia causes polyuria and thirst by impairing the kidney's ability to concentrate urine.

stem:
A 44-year-old woman on carbimazole for Graves' disease is seen at the endocrine clinic. She has mild redness of the conjunctivae and her eyes have become slightly more prominent. She works in a café, wears reading glasses, drinks plenty of water and goes running twice a week. She also smokes about fifteen cigarettes a day.

Which modifiable factor is most strongly linked to her eye disease getting worse?
why_correct: Smoking is the most important modifiable risk factor for developing thyroid eye disease and for it becoming more severe. It also reduces the response to treatment and increases the risk of eye disease worsening after radioactive iodine. She should be strongly advised and supported to stop smoking.
why_wrong: B. Fluid intake has no effect on thyroid eye disease. C. Regular exercise does not worsen the condition. D. Dietary fibre is not a recognised risk factor. E. Wearing glasses does not influence the course of orbital inflammation.
pearl: Radioactive iodine can worsen thyroid eye disease, particularly in smokers, so steroid cover may be considered when it is given.
thinking: Graves' disease with mild eye involvement ↓ Look for modifiable factors ↓ Smoking increases orbital inflammation ↓ It worsens severity and treatment response ↓ Offer smoking cessation support
exam_trap: C, Running several times a week — exertion may seem to raise orbital pressure, but exercise has no recognised link with thyroid eye disease.
takeaway: Stopping smoking is the key modifiable step to protect patients with Graves' disease from worsening eye disease.

stem:
A 56-year-old man tells his GP that for several months he has felt sluggish, has put on weight and needs to wear a jumper when others are comfortable. He is also opening his bowels less often. He has never had thyroid problems, is clinically stable and is not taking any regular medicines.

What is the most appropriate first step to assess his thyroid function?

options.B: Request an ultrasound of the neck before blood tests
options.C: Arrange a radioisotope thyroid uptake scan
options.E: Measure free T3 on its own

why_correct: In a stable adult with symptoms suggesting primary thyroid dysfunction, NICE advises measuring TSH as the first-line test. TSH is the most sensitive marker of primary thyroid disease, and free T4 is added if the TSH is abnormal. His tiredness, weight gain, cold intolerance and constipation suggest hypothyroidism, which TSH will detect.
why_wrong: A. TPO antibodies help explain the cause once thyroid dysfunction is found, not as the first test. B. Ultrasound assesses structure, such as nodules or goitre, not function. C. Uptake scanning is used to find the cause of confirmed hyperthyroidism. E. Free T3 alone is not used to detect hypothyroidism and may stay normal until late.
pearl: Do not rely on TSH alone if secondary (pituitary) hypothyroidism is suspected, as TSH may be low or normal despite a low free T4.
thinking: Symptoms suggest hypothyroidism ↓ Adult, clinically stable, no thyroid history ↓ Primary thyroid disease is most likely ↓ TSH is the most sensitive first test ↓ Add free T4 if TSH is abnormal
exam_trap: A, Check thyroid peroxidase antibodies first — autoimmune thyroiditis is the common cause, but antibodies identify the cause rather than whether thyroid function is abnormal.
takeaway: When primary thyroid dysfunction is suspected in a stable adult, TSH is the first test.

stem:
A 34-year-old woman comes to the GP because her periods have become much heavier over the last six months, and she is now flooding through protection. On questioning she also reports constant tiredness, a gain in weight despite a poor appetite, hard stools and always feeling cold. Her skin is dry.

Which endocrine disorder best explains all of her symptoms?
why_correct: Hypothyroidism slows metabolism, causing fatigue, weight gain, constipation, cold intolerance and dry skin. It also commonly disturbs the menstrual cycle, and menorrhagia is a recognised feature in women. Thyroid function tests should be part of the work-up for heavy menstrual bleeding when other features suggest this.
why_wrong: A. Acromegaly causes coarse features, enlarged hands and feet and sweating, not cold intolerance. C. Hyperthyroidism usually causes weight loss, heat intolerance, loose stools and lighter periods. D. Phaeochromocytoma causes episodic headache, sweating and palpitations. E. Diabetes insipidus causes polyuria and thirst.
pearl: NICE advises testing thyroid function in heavy menstrual bleeding only when there are other signs or symptoms of thyroid disease.
thinking: Heavy periods plus systemic symptoms ↓ Tiredness, weight gain, cold intolerance, constipation, dry skin ↓ Points to a slowed metabolism ↓ Hypothyroidism also causes menorrhagia ↓ Check thyroid function
exam_trap: C, Overactive thyroid — any thyroid disease can disturb periods, but hyperthyroidism tends to cause lighter periods with weight loss and heat intolerance.
takeaway: Menorrhagia with fatigue, weight gain and cold intolerance should prompt testing for hypothyroidism.

stem:
A 27-year-old man with vitiligo sees his GP because he keeps feeling faint when he stands up and has lost weight over three months. His partner says he looks tanned although he has not been on holiday, and the creases of his palms are darker than before. Blood tests show a low sodium and a high potassium.

What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.A: Syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion

why_correct: Autoimmune destruction of the adrenal cortex causes loss of both cortisol and aldosterone. Aldosterone deficiency produces sodium loss, potassium retention and postural hypotension, while low cortisol drives up ACTH, which causes pigmentation of skin creases and sun-exposed areas. Coexisting autoimmune disease such as vitiligo supports Addison's disease.
why_wrong: A. SIADH causes hyponatraemia with normal potassium and no pigmentation or postural hypotension. B. Phaeochromocytoma causes episodic hypertension, not postural hypotension. C. Conn syndrome causes hypertension and hypokalaemia. E. ACTH-dependent Cushing's can cause pigmentation, but cortisol excess gives hypertension and hypokalaemia rather than postural hypotension and hyperkalaemia.
pearl: Suspected adrenal crisis should be treated with immediate intravenous or intramuscular hydrocortisone without waiting for test results.
thinking: Postural dizziness and weight loss ↓ New pigmentation of palmar creases ↓ Low sodium with high potassium ↓ Cortisol and aldosterone both deficient ↓ Primary adrenal insufficiency, likely autoimmune
exam_trap: A, Syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion — it causes hyponatraemia, but potassium is normal and there is no pigmentation or postural drop.
takeaway: Hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia, postural hypotension and pigmentation together suggest Addison's disease.
notes: Reviewer fix: why_wrong E corrected: ACTH-dependent Cushing's distinguished by hypertension/hypokalaemia, not 'weight gain' (ectopic ACTH often causes weight loss).

stem:
An 81-year-old woman in a care home has become slower and more forgetful over the winter. Staff note that she has gained weight, her voice has become hoarse, and she asks for extra blankets. Her GP sends thyroid function tests, suspecting that her thyroid gland itself is failing.

Which result would confirm primary hypothyroidism?

options.A: Low TSH with high free T4
options.B: High TSH with low free T4
options.C: Low TSH with low free T4
options.D: Normal TSH with high free T4
options.E: High TSH with high free T4

correct_answer: B. High TSH with low free T4
why_correct: In primary hypothyroidism the thyroid gland cannot make enough thyroxine, so free T4 falls. The intact pituitary responds to the loss of negative feedback by increasing TSH. A raised TSH with a low free T4 is therefore the expected pattern.
why_wrong: A. Low TSH with high free T4 indicates primary hyperthyroidism. C. Low TSH with low free T4 suggests pituitary failure (secondary hypothyroidism) or non-thyroidal illness. D. Normal TSH with high free T4 may suggest assay interference, a TSH-secreting tumour or thyroid hormone resistance. E. High TSH with high free T4 is unusual and suggests a TSH-secreting tumour, hormone resistance or assay interference.
pearl: In older people or those with heart disease, levothyroxine is started at a low dose and increased slowly.
thinking: Insidious slowing, weight gain, cold intolerance ↓ Suspected failure of the thyroid gland itself ↓ Low T4 removes negative feedback ↓ Pituitary increases TSH ↓ High TSH, low free T4
exam_trap: C, Low TSH with low free T4 — both values point to hypothyroidism, but a low TSH means the pituitary is the failing gland, not the thyroid.
takeaway: Primary hypothyroidism shows a high TSH with a low free T4.

stem:
A 71-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes for over twenty years has her annual review with the practice nurse. Monofilament testing shows she cannot feel the filament at several sites on both soles, and she admits she did not notice a blister on her heel until her daughter saw it.

Which complication is she now at particular risk of?

options.A: Inflammation of the external ear canal
options.E: Cataract as her only eye problem

why_correct: Peripheral neuropathy removes protective sensation, so pressure, burns and small injuries go unnoticed. Unprotected trauma, often combined with poor circulation and impaired healing, leads to foot ulceration. Loss of monofilament sensation places her in a higher-risk category needing regular foot protection input.
why_wrong: A. Otitis externa is not a consequence of peripheral neuropathy, although severe forms occur in diabetes. B. Migraine is unrelated to diabetic neuropathy. D. Appendicitis is not linked to loss of foot sensation. E. Diabetes raises the risk of cataract and retinopathy, but this is not what reduced foot sensation predicts.
pearl: NICE recommends that everyone with diabetes has their feet assessed at least annually, including monofilament testing, and that risk is classified to guide follow-up.
thinking: Long-standing diabetes ↓ Loss of monofilament sensation on both feet ↓ Unnoticed blister shows loss of protective sensation ↓ Minor injuries go undetected ↓ High risk of foot ulceration
exam_trap: A, Inflammation of the external ear canal — malignant otitis externa is a recognised diabetic complication, but it is not caused by loss of sensation in the feet.
takeaway: Loss of protective sensation in diabetes markedly increases the risk of foot ulceration.

stem:
A 59-year-old man with type 1 diabetes and loss of feeling in both feet is seen in the diabetes clinic. He lives alone and asks what he should be doing at home to look after his feet.

What is the most important advice to give?

options.A: Pare away hard skin yourself with a razor blade
options.B: Use medicated corn plasters on sore spots
options.C: Inspect the feet every day and protect them from injury
options.D: Go barefoot indoors to help retrain sensation
options.E: Check the bath temperature by dipping a foot in

correct_answer: C. Inspect the feet every day and protect them from injury
why_correct: With reduced sensation he will not feel minor injuries, so daily inspection (using a mirror or help if needed) allows problems to be spotted early. He should wear well-fitting footwear, avoid going barefoot and seek prompt advice for any break in the skin. These measures reduce the risk of ulceration and amputation.
why_wrong: A. Cutting hard skin at home risks wounds he cannot feel; this should be done by a podiatrist. B. Corn plasters contain acids that can cause skin breakdown and ulcers in a neuropathic foot. D. Walking barefoot exposes insensate feet to unnoticed trauma and does not restore sensation. E. An insensate foot cannot judge temperature, so this risks scald injuries; water should be tested with the elbow or a thermometer.
pearl: Any new foot ulcer, colour change or swelling in a person with diabetes should be reported promptly, as delay worsens outcomes.
thinking: Diabetes with loss of protective sensation ↓ Injuries may go unnoticed ↓ Early detection prevents ulcer progression ↓ Daily self-inspection and protective footwear ↓ Avoid self-treatment and barefoot walking
exam_trap: B, Use medicated corn plasters on sore spots — they seem like simple self-care, but the acid can burn the skin and start an ulcer in an insensate foot.
takeaway: People with diabetic neuropathy should check their feet daily and protect them from injury.

stem:
A 66-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes phones the practice because she has found a small open sore on the underside of her big toe while drying her feet. It does not hurt and she cannot recall injuring it. She asks whether she should just keep an eye on it.

What is the most appropriate approach?

options.A: Soak the foot in hot water each day to clean the sore
options.B: Moisturise the area and rest at home
options.C: Review only if it becomes painful or starts to discharge
options.D: Arrange prompt assessment of the diabetic foot
options.E: Cover with gauze and book a GP review in a month

correct_answer: D. Arrange prompt assessment of the diabetic foot
why_correct: A new foot ulcer in someone with diabetes is a diabetic foot problem that needs prompt assessment, because neuropathy, ischaemia and infection can progress quickly. NICE advises urgent referral to the multidisciplinary foot care service or foot protection service. The absence of pain does not mean the ulcer is minor; it reflects reduced sensation.
why_wrong: A. Hot water soaks risk scalds and skin maceration in an insensate foot. B. Moisturiser and rest do not address infection, ischaemia or offloading. C. Waiting for pain is unsafe because neuropathy masks pain. E. Delaying review by weeks allows infection and tissue loss to progress.
pearl: Painlessness in a diabetic foot ulcer reflects neuropathy and should not be taken as reassurance.
thinking: New ulcer on a diabetic foot ↓ Painless because of neuropathy ↓ Risk of infection, ischaemia and amputation ↓ Needs urgent specialist foot assessment ↓ Do not watch and wait
exam_trap: C, Review only if it becomes painful or starts to discharge — it sounds proportionate for a small sore, but neuropathy hides pain and infection may already be developing.
takeaway: Any new foot ulcer in a person with diabetes needs prompt specialist foot assessment.

stem:
A 62-year-old woman with poorly controlled type 2 diabetes is noticed by her podiatrist to have a punched-out sore under the head of the first metatarsal, surrounded by thick callus. She had not felt it. Pedal pulses are easily palpable and she has a glove-and-stocking loss of sensation.

What is the most likely cause of the lesion?

options.B: Venous ulcer from chronic venous insufficiency
options.E: Acute gout of the big toe joint

why_correct: Neuropathic ulcers develop at pressure points on the sole, such as under the metatarsal heads, often with surrounding callus. Loss of protective sensation means they are painless and unnoticed. Palpable pulses argue against an ischaemic cause, so this is a neuropathic diabetic foot ulcer.
why_wrong: A. Tinea pedis causes itchy scaling between the toes, not a deep plantar ulcer. B. Venous ulcers occur in the gaiter area above the ankle. C. A verruca is a painful raised lesion with dark capillary dots, not an ulcer. E. Gout causes an acutely painful, red, swollen joint rather than a painless ulcer.
pearl: Offloading pressure from the ulcer, for example with a cast or specialist footwear, is central to healing a neuropathic ulcer.
thinking: Diabetes with glove-and-stocking sensory loss ↓ Painless ulcer at a plantar pressure point ↓ Surrounding callus ↓ Good pulses make ischaemia less likely ↓ Neuropathic ulcer
exam_trap: C, Plantar wart — a callused lesion on the sole can resemble a verruca, but warts are painful and do not form punched-out ulcers.
takeaway: A painless ulcer with callus over a plantar pressure point in diabetes is neuropathic until proven otherwise.

stem:
A 24-year-old woman with irregular periods attends a sexual health clinic. She is upset about thick, dark hairs that have appeared on her upper lip, chin and between her breasts over the past year and that she has to remove regularly. Her voice and muscle bulk are unchanged.

Which term best describes this hair pattern?

options.A: Diffuse hair shedding after a stressor
options.B: Excess fine hair in a non-androgenic distribution
options.C: Masculinisation with deep voice and clitoromegaly

why_correct: Hirsutism means excess coarse terminal hair in a male-pattern, androgen-dependent distribution in a woman, such as the face, chest and lower abdomen. Combined with irregular periods, the most common cause is polycystic ovary syndrome. The absence of voice change or increased muscle bulk argues against virilisation.
why_wrong: A. Telogen effluvium is diffuse scalp hair shedding after illness or stress. B. Hypertrichosis is excess hair not confined to androgen-dependent areas, often from drugs or other causes. C. Virilisation includes deepening voice, clitoromegaly and increased muscle bulk, which she does not have. E. Alopecia describes hair loss, not excess hair.
pearl: Rapid onset hirsutism with virilisation should prompt investigation for an androgen-secreting ovarian or adrenal tumour.
thinking: Coarse dark hair on face and chest ↓ Androgen-dependent, male-pattern distribution ↓ No voice change or muscle gain ↓ Not virilisation ↓ Hirsutism, likely PCOS with irregular periods
exam_trap: C, Masculinisation with deep voice and clitoromegaly — male-pattern hair suggests androgen excess, but virilisation requires extra features she does not have.
takeaway: Hirsutism is male-pattern coarse terminal hair growth in a woman.

stem:
A 57-year-old taxi driver with type 2 diabetes has an HbA1c that has remained well above his agreed target for three years despite metformin and gliclazide. He feels well and asks the practice nurse why it matters if he has no symptoms.

Which long-term consequence of sustained hyperglycaemia is most important to explain?

options.C: Damage to small blood vessels of the eyes, kidneys and nerves

correct_answer: C. Damage to small blood vessels of the eyes, kidneys and nerves
why_correct: Sustained hyperglycaemia damages small blood vessels, leading to retinopathy, nephropathy and neuropathy. These complications develop silently over years, which is why good glycaemic control matters even when the patient feels well. Better control reduces the risk of these microvascular complications.
why_wrong: A. Renal colic is not a characteristic complication of diabetes, and nothing occurs in every patient. B. Otitis externa can be severe in diabetes but is not the key long-term consequence of poor control. D. Cataract is more common in diabetes but does not develop in every patient. E. Appendicitis is not linked to glycaemic control.
pearl: Annual diabetic review should include retinal screening, urine albumin to creatinine ratio, eGFR and foot assessment to detect microvascular damage early.
thinking: Persistently raised HbA1c ↓ Patient asymptomatic ↓ Hyperglycaemia damages small vessels over years ↓ Retinopathy, nephropathy, neuropathy ↓ Explain the value of improving control
exam_trap: D, Cataract in every patient — diabetes does increase cataract risk, but no complication is universal and microvascular damage is the key concern.
takeaway: Sustained hyperglycaemia causes microvascular damage to the eyes, kidneys and nerves.

stem:
A 41-year-old man has blood pressure that remains high despite three antihypertensives. He complains of muscle weakness and needing to pass urine at night. His potassium has been low on repeated checks although he takes no diuretic, and further tests show a high aldosterone level with suppressed renin.

What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.B: Syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion

why_correct: Autonomous aldosterone production causes sodium and water retention, raising blood pressure, and increases renal potassium loss, causing hypokalaemia with weakness and nocturia. The high aldosterone with suppressed renin confirms the excess is primary rather than driven by the renin system. Resistant hypertension with low potassium is a classic trigger to screen for this.
why_wrong: A. Addison's disease causes hypotension and hyperkalaemia. B. SIADH causes hyponatraemia without hypertension or hypokalaemia. C. Hypoparathyroidism causes hypocalcaemia, not hypertension. D. Cushing's syndrome can cause hypertension and hypokalaemia, but aldosterone would not be primarily raised and there are no cushingoid features.
pearl: Primary hyperaldosteronism is one of the most common causes of secondary hypertension and should be considered in resistant or early-onset hypertension.
thinking: Resistant hypertension ↓ Unprovoked hypokalaemia ↓ High aldosterone with suppressed renin ↓ Autonomous adrenal aldosterone production ↓ Primary hyperaldosteronism
exam_trap: D, Cushing's syndrome — cortisol excess can cause hypertension and low potassium, but the biochemistry points specifically to autonomous aldosterone.
takeaway: Hypertension with hypokalaemia and a high aldosterone to renin ratio suggests primary hyperaldosteronism.

stem:
A 33-year-old woman attending a preconception clinic is found to have a very high blood pressure. She describes spells of pounding headache, drenching sweats and a racing heart lasting a few minutes at a time. Imaging shows an adrenal mass and phaeochromocytoma is suspected.

Which substance is the tumour producing in excess?
why_correct: Phaeochromocytomas arise from chromaffin cells of the adrenal medulla and secrete adrenaline, noradrenaline and sometimes dopamine. Surges of catecholamines cause paroxysmal headache, sweating, palpitations and hypertension. Diagnosis is by plasma or urinary metanephrines.
why_wrong: A. Parathyroid hormone excess causes hypercalcaemia, not paroxysmal hypertension. B. Thyroxine excess causes persistent rather than episodic symptoms with weight loss and heat intolerance. C. Cortisol comes from the adrenal cortex and causes cushingoid features. E. Aldosterone comes from the adrenal cortex and causes sustained hypertension with hypokalaemia.
pearl: Alpha-blockade must be established before any beta-blocker is given, to avoid unopposed alpha stimulation and a hypertensive crisis.
thinking: Paroxysmal headache, sweating, palpitations ↓ Severe hypertension ↓ Adrenal medullary tumour ↓ Chromaffin cells secrete catecholamines ↓ Confirm with metanephrines
exam_trap: C, Cortisol alone — the tumour is adrenal, but phaeochromocytoma arises in the medulla, while cortisol comes from the cortex.
takeaway: Phaeochromocytoma causes episodic symptoms through excess catecholamine secretion.

stem:
A doctor on the endocrine ward is reviewing a 49-year-old woman just diagnosed with an aldosterone-secreting adrenal adenoma. She has hypertension and a low potassium. While explaining the renin-angiotensin system to her, the doctor is asked what her kidneys are doing in response.

In this condition, what happens to renin secretion?

options.D: It becomes entirely independent of blood pressure

why_correct: Autonomous aldosterone production causes sodium retention and expansion of the circulating volume. The juxtaglomerular cells sense increased renal perfusion and reduce renin release. This suppressed renin with high aldosterone is the basis of the aldosterone to renin ratio used in screening.
why_wrong: A. Renin rises in secondary hyperaldosteronism, such as renal artery stenosis or heart failure, not in primary disease. C. There is no sleep-specific rise in renin in this condition. D. Renin release still responds to renal perfusion; it is suppressed, not independent. E. Persistently high renin would suggest a secondary cause.
pearl: Many antihypertensives, including ACE inhibitors, beta-blockers and diuretics, alter renin and can affect the aldosterone to renin ratio.
thinking: Aldosterone made autonomously ↓ Sodium and water retained ↓ Circulating volume expands ↓ Kidney senses increased perfusion ↓ Renin is suppressed
exam_trap: A, It rises markedly — high aldosterone and high renin go together in secondary hyperaldosteronism, but in primary disease renin is suppressed.
takeaway: In primary hyperaldosteronism aldosterone is high and renin is suppressed.

stem:
A 46-year-old woman with hard-to-control hypertension and a low potassium has adrenal imaging showing a single left adrenal nodule. Adrenal vein sampling confirms that the nodule is the source of excess aldosterone.

Which eponymous name is given to this condition?
why_correct: Conn syndrome describes primary hyperaldosteronism, classically due to a unilateral aldosterone-producing adrenal adenoma. It causes hypertension and hypokalaemia with suppressed renin. A lateralised adenoma can often be treated by laparoscopic adrenalectomy.
why_wrong: A. Addison's disease is primary adrenal insufficiency with low aldosterone and cortisol. C. Sheehan syndrome is pituitary infarction after postpartum haemorrhage. D. Graves' disease is autoimmune hyperthyroidism. E. Cushing syndrome is due to cortisol excess.
pearl: Bilateral adrenal hyperplasia is treated medically with a mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist such as spironolactone rather than surgery.
thinking: Resistant hypertension with low potassium ↓ Unilateral adrenal nodule ↓ Venous sampling confirms it as the aldosterone source ↓ Aldosterone-producing adenoma ↓ Conn syndrome
exam_trap: E, Cushing syndrome — it is another adrenal eponym linked with hypertension and low potassium, but it refers to cortisol rather than aldosterone excess.
takeaway: Conn syndrome is primary hyperaldosteronism due to an aldosterone-producing adrenal adenoma.

stem:
A 52-year-old man is referred by his GP with high blood pressure and weakness. A CT scan shows a right adrenal adenoma, and tests confirm it is secreting excess aldosterone. His arterial blood gas is being interpreted alongside his electrolytes.

Which additional biochemical abnormality is most likely?
why_correct: Aldosterone acts on the distal nephron to reabsorb sodium in exchange for potassium and hydrogen ions. Excess aldosterone therefore causes hypokalaemia and loss of hydrogen ions in the urine, producing a metabolic alkalosis. Hypokalaemia itself also shifts hydrogen ions into cells, worsening the alkalosis.
why_wrong: A. Hydrogen ion loss causes alkalosis, not acidosis. B. Potassium is lost in the urine, so hypokalaemia is expected. D. Hypoglycaemia is not a feature; hypokalaemia may in fact impair insulin secretion. E. Sodium is usually normal or high-normal because of aldosterone escape.
pearl: Sodium is usually normal in primary hyperaldosteronism because of aldosterone escape, so a normal sodium does not exclude it.
thinking: Aldosterone-secreting adrenal adenoma ↓ Distal sodium reabsorption increases ↓ Potassium and hydrogen ions lost in urine ↓ Hypokalaemia drives further hydrogen ion shift ↓ Metabolic alkalosis
exam_trap: E, Marked hyponatraemia — adrenal disease is often linked with low sodium, but that is Addison's disease; aldosterone excess retains sodium.
takeaway: Primary hyperaldosteronism causes hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis.

stem:
A 42-year-old woman develops tingling around her mouth and fingertips on the day after a total thyroidectomy. On the surgical ward, the doctor taps just in front of her ear over the course of a cranial nerve and sees the corner of her mouth twitch.

What is this examination finding called?
why_correct: Chvostek sign is twitching of the facial muscles when the facial nerve is tapped anterior to the ear. It reflects neuromuscular irritability from hypocalcaemia. After thyroidectomy, damage to or removal of the parathyroid glands is a common cause of low calcium.
why_wrong: A. Kernig sign is pain or resistance on knee extension with the hip flexed, seen in meningism. B. Romberg sign is loss of balance with eyes closed, indicating proprioceptive loss. C. Murphy sign is arrest of inspiration on palpation of the right upper quadrant in cholecystitis. D. Babinski sign is an extensor plantar response from an upper motor neurone lesion.
pearl: Trousseau sign, carpal spasm after inflating a blood pressure cuff, is more specific for hypocalcaemia than Chvostek sign.
thinking: Perioral and fingertip tingling after thyroidectomy ↓ Suspect parathyroid injury and hypocalcaemia ↓ Tap facial nerve in front of the ear ↓ Facial muscles twitch ↓ Chvostek sign
exam_trap: D, Babinski sign — it is another eponymous neurological reflex, but it tests the plantar response for an upper motor neurone lesion.
takeaway: Facial twitching on tapping the facial nerve is Chvostek sign, a marker of hypocalcaemia.

presentation: Acute hypoglycaemia in a non-diabetic adult
stem:
A 52-year-old warehouse supervisor with no history of diabetes is brought to the staff first-aid room after colleagues notice he has become pale, clammy, shaky and muddled mid-shift. He has had similar spells before lunch over recent weeks. He is drowsy but rousable, responds to his name and can swallow safely. A finger-prick test shows a glucose of 2.6 mmol/L.

Which immediate step should be taken first?

options.A: Arrange admission for a supervised prolonged fast
options.C: Give oral propranolol to settle the tremor and sweating
options.D: Advise him to follow a low-carbohydrate diet
options.E: Give fast-acting oral carbohydrate such as glucose tablets or a sugary drink

correct_answer: E. Give fast-acting oral carbohydrate such as glucose tablets or a sugary drink
why_correct: He has symptomatic hypoglycaemia and can still swallow safely, so the first priority is to raise his glucose with a quick-acting oral carbohydrate, then recheck after about 15 minutes and follow with a longer-acting snack. The cause of recurrent hypoglycaemia in a person not on glucose-lowering drugs needs investigation later, but only once the acute episode has been corrected.
why_wrong: A. A supervised fast helps find the cause, such as an insulinoma, but does nothing for the current low glucose. B. Hydrocortisone is for suspected adrenal crisis, which is not the picture here. C. Propranolol would mask the warning symptoms and does not raise glucose. D. Cutting carbohydrate would worsen the immediate problem.
pearl: If a hypoglycaemic adult cannot swallow safely or is unconscious, give intravenous glucose (or intramuscular glucagon if IV access is not available) rather than anything by mouth.
thinking: Sweating, tremor and confusion ↓ Capillary glucose clearly low ↓ Conscious and able to swallow ↓ Treat the low glucose first with fast oral carbohydrate ↓ Investigate the cause afterwards
exam_trap: A, Admission for a prolonged fast — investigating a possible insulinoma feels thorough, but diagnostic work-up never comes before correcting the low glucose in front of you.
takeaway: Correct symptomatic hypoglycaemia immediately, using oral fast-acting glucose if the patient can swallow, before looking for the cause.

stem:
A 37-year-old man is brought to the emergency department by his partner after two days of profuse diarrhoea. He takes hydrocortisone and fludrocortisone for autoimmune adrenal failure diagnosed three years ago. He now has central abdominal pain, feels faint whenever he sits up, and is cold, clammy and slow to answer questions. His blood pressure is low and does not improve when he lies flat.

What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: He has known primary adrenal insufficiency and an intercurrent gut illness that will have stopped him absorbing his oral steroids and increased his cortisol needs. Hypotension with abdominal pain, weakness and confusion in this setting is an adrenal crisis until proven otherwise. It is a medical emergency requiring immediate parenteral hydrocortisone and intravenous fluids.
why_wrong: B. Gastroenteritis is the trigger, but persistent hypotension and confusion in someone with adrenal failure point to cortisol deficiency, not just fluid loss. C. There is no history of diabetes and nothing to suggest ketosis. D. Thyroid storm causes fever, tachyarrhythmia and agitation rather than this picture. E. Appendicitis would not explain shock out of proportion to the illness in a patient dependent on steroid replacement.
pearl: Adrenal crisis can cause abdominal pain severe enough to mimic a surgical abdomen, which can delay recognition if the steroid history is missed.
thinking: Known Addison's disease on replacement ↓ Diarrhoeal illness stops oral absorption and raises demand ↓ Hypotension, abdominal pain, confusion ↓ Cortisol deficiency decompensating ↓ Adrenal crisis
exam_trap: B, Viral gastroenteritis with simple dehydration — the diarrhoea is real and obvious, but it is the trigger rather than the diagnosis; treating it as dehydration alone misses a life-threatening crisis.
takeaway: In anyone on steroid replacement, intercurrent illness with hypotension and abdominal pain is an adrenal crisis until proven otherwise.

stem:
A 29-year-old woman sees her GP with several months of exhaustion, nausea and craving for salty food. She has lost weight, and her palmar creases and inner cheeks look darker than before. Her blood pressure drops noticeably when she stands. The GP suspects primary failure of the adrenal glands and requests urea and electrolytes.

Which result would most support this diagnosis?
why_correct: Destruction of the adrenal cortex removes aldosterone as well as cortisol. Without aldosterone the distal nephron cannot excrete potassium or retain sodium, so the classic pattern is hyperkalaemia with hyponatraemia. Her pigmentation, salt craving and postural hypotension all fit primary adrenal insufficiency.
why_wrong: A. Low potassium suggests aldosterone excess or losses such as vomiting, not adrenal failure. B. A metabolic alkalosis goes with mineralocorticoid excess; adrenal failure tends towards a mild acidosis. C. Sodium falls rather than rises as it is lost in the urine. E. Low phosphate is not a feature of adrenal insufficiency.
pearl: Hyperkalaemia points to primary adrenal failure; in secondary (pituitary) failure aldosterone is preserved via renin-angiotensin, so potassium is usually normal and there is no pigmentation.
thinking: Fatigue, weight loss, salt craving ↓ Skin and buccal pigmentation suggest high ACTH ↓ Primary adrenal failure loses aldosterone ↓ Potassium retained, sodium lost ↓ Hyperkalaemia
exam_trap: A, Hypokalaemia — potassium disturbance is expected in adrenal disease, so it is easy to pick the wrong direction; low potassium belongs to Conn's syndrome, the opposite state.
takeaway: Primary adrenal insufficiency classically causes hyperkalaemia and hyponatraemia due to aldosterone deficiency.

stem:
A 63-year-old retired builder takes daily hydrocortisone after surgery for a pituitary adenoma left him with hypopituitarism. He telephones his GP practice on a Saturday morning. Since last night he has had shivers, aching muscles and a fever, and he thinks he has flu. He is drinking and eating small amounts and has not vomited. He asks what he should do with his tablets.

Which advice is most appropriate?

options.A: Stop the hydrocortisone until the fever has gone
options.B: Keep taking exactly the same dose as usual
options.C: Halve the dose to reduce the risk of the infection spreading
options.D: Change from hydrocortisone to fludrocortisone for the duration of the illness
options.E: Increase his glucocorticoid dose according to his sick day rules and seek urgent help or use his emergency injection if he starts vomiting

correct_answer: E. Increase his glucocorticoid dose according to his sick day rules and seek urgent help or use his emergency injection if he starts vomiting
why_correct: Someone on long-term steroid replacement cannot increase their own cortisol output in response to illness. During a febrile illness he should follow his sick day rules, which typically means doubling the daily glucocorticoid dose until he is better. If he vomits or cannot keep tablets down he needs injected hydrocortisone and urgent assessment to prevent an adrenal crisis.
why_wrong: A. Stopping replacement during stress is the classic trigger for adrenal crisis. B. The usual dose does not cover the extra cortisol needed during a fever. C. Reducing the dose increases the risk of crisis and does not help fight infection. D. Fludrocortisone replaces aldosterone, not cortisol, and is not part of pituitary-related steroid replacement.
pearl: Everyone on steroid replacement should carry a steroid emergency card and, for primary or secondary adrenal insufficiency, an emergency hydrocortisone injection kit with training in its use.
thinking: On hydrocortisone replacement ↓ Cannot mount a stress cortisol response ↓ Febrile illness increases cortisol need ↓ Double the dose per sick day rules ↓ Injection and urgent review if vomiting
exam_trap: A, Stopping the hydrocortisone — patients often worry that steroids weaken the immune system, but withholding replacement during illness can precipitate adrenal crisis.
