takeaway: During intercurrent febrile illness, patients on steroid replacement should increase their dose according to sick day rules and get urgent help if vomiting.

stem:
A 68-year-old woman on a care of the elderly ward has severe vitamin D deficiency and poor oral intake. Overnight she complains of tingling in her fingers and around her lips and painful cramps in her calves. Her adjusted calcium is markedly low, with normal potassium and magnesium. A 12-lead ECG is recorded.

Which abnormality is most likely to be seen?
why_correct: Low calcium lengthens phase 2 of the ventricular action potential, which prolongs the ST segment and therefore the QT interval. This matters because a long QT predisposes to ventricular arrhythmias, so symptomatic hypocalcaemia with QT prolongation needs prompt intravenous calcium replacement and cardiac monitoring.
why_wrong: B. A short QT is the ECG sign of high calcium. C. Tall tented T waves are seen with hyperkalaemia, and her potassium is normal. D. Prominent U waves suggest hypokalaemia. E. Delta waves indicate a pre-excitation pathway as in Wolff-Parkinson-White, not an electrolyte problem.
pearl: Hypomagnesaemia often coexists with hypocalcaemia and must be corrected, otherwise the calcium will not stay up.
thinking: Perioral and finger tingling with cramps ↓ Adjusted calcium low ↓ Calcium affects ventricular repolarisation ↓ Lengthened ST segment ↓ Prolonged QT
exam_trap: B, Shortened QT interval — it is easy to mix up which direction calcium shifts the QT; remember that a low calcium gives a long QT.
takeaway: Hypocalcaemia prolongs the QT interval, while hypercalcaemia shortens it.

stem:
A 19-year-old university fresher with recently diagnosed type 1 diabetes arrives at the emergency department after a day of vomiting and abdominal pain. He is breathing deeply and rapidly, and his blood ketones are very high. A venous gas shows a low pH and a low bicarbonate. Before any treatment is started, the registrar asks what the calculated anion gap will show.

Which finding is expected?

options.B: A normal anion gap with a high chloride
options.E: A raised partial pressure of carbon dioxide

why_correct: In diabetic ketoacidosis, ketoacids such as beta-hydroxybutyrate accumulate and are not measured in the routine electrolyte calculation. As they consume bicarbonate, the gap between measured cations and anions widens, producing a high anion gap metabolic acidosis. His deep sighing (Kussmaul) breathing is respiratory compensation for this acidosis.
why_wrong: B. A normal-gap, high-chloride acidosis is seen with diarrhoea, renal tubular acidosis or large volumes of 0.9% sodium chloride, and can appear later in DKA treatment, but not at presentation. C. A low anion gap occurs in states such as hypoalbuminaemia, not ketoacidosis. D. Bicarbonate is consumed, so it falls. E. Rapid deep breathing lowers carbon dioxide as compensation.
pearl: During DKA treatment, a persisting acidosis with falling ketones and a rising chloride often reflects hyperchloraemic acidosis from saline rather than ongoing ketosis.
thinking: Type 1 diabetes with vomiting and Kussmaul breathing ↓ High ketones, low pH, low bicarbonate ↓ Ketoacids are unmeasured anions ↓ Gap between measured cations and anions widens ↓ High anion gap metabolic acidosis
exam_trap: B, A normal anion gap with a high chloride — this pattern does occur in DKA, but only later during treatment with large volumes of saline, not in the untreated patient.
takeaway: Untreated diabetic ketoacidosis causes a high anion gap metabolic acidosis because ketoacids are unmeasured anions.

stem:
A 57-year-old taxi driver with type 2 diabetes attends a medication review with the practice pharmacist. He is puzzled because his finger-prick reading this morning was close to normal, yet his recent HbA1c was reported as above his agreed target. He asks what the HbA1c result actually tells him.

Which explanation is most accurate?

options.A: It shows his fasting glucose on the morning the blood was taken
options.B: It shows his average glucose over the last fortnight
options.C: It reflects the highest glucose peaks after meals in the previous week
options.D: It reflects his average glucose over roughly the previous two to three months
options.E: It measures how much insulin his pancreas is still producing

correct_answer: D. It reflects his average glucose over roughly the previous two to three months
why_correct: Glucose attaches irreversibly to haemoglobin in circulating red cells, and the proportion of glycated haemoglobin depends on the glucose levels those cells have been exposed to over their lifespan of about 120 days. HbA1c therefore reflects average glucose over roughly the past two to three months, weighted towards the most recent weeks, which explains why a single good morning reading can coexist with a raised HbA1c.
why_wrong: A. A single fasting value is a snapshot and is not what HbA1c measures. B. Fructosamine reflects the previous two to three weeks, not HbA1c. C. HbA1c is an average and does not isolate post-meal peaks. E. Insulin production is assessed with C-peptide, not HbA1c.
pearl: Anything that shortens red cell survival, such as haemolysis, recent blood loss or transfusion, falsely lowers HbA1c, while iron deficiency can falsely raise it.
thinking: Patient confused by normal morning reading ↓ HbA1c is glycation of haemoglobin ↓ Depends on red cell lifespan ↓ Integrates glucose exposure over weeks to months ↓ Average over about two to three months
exam_trap: B, Average glucose over the last fortnight — this describes fructosamine, which is a short-term glycated protein marker and is easily confused with HbA1c.
takeaway: HbA1c reflects average blood glucose over the preceding two to three months, in line with red cell lifespan.

stem:
A 41-year-old man with type 2 diabetes is known to carry an inherited haemoglobin variant. At his review his HbA1c has been within his target range for over a year, yet the readings from his continuous glucose monitor show glucose persistently well above range most of the day, and he describes thirst and passing urine at night. His sensor readings have been checked against finger-prick tests and are accurate.

What is the most appropriate next step?

options.A: Accept the HbA1c, as it is the gold-standard marker of control
options.B: Repeat the HbA1c every month until it matches the monitor
options.C: Relax his HbA1c target to allow for the haemoglobin variant
options.D: Stop the glucose monitor, as it is giving misleading results
options.E: Recognise the HbA1c may be unreliable and use alternative measures of glucose control

correct_answer: E. Recognise the HbA1c may be unreliable and use alternative measures of glucose control
why_correct: Haemoglobin variants and conditions that alter red cell lifespan can make HbA1c inaccurate, depending on the laboratory method. When the HbA1c disagrees with symptoms and reliable glucose readings, NICE advises investigating the discrepancy and using other measures such as capillary or continuous glucose monitoring, or fructosamine, to guide treatment. Here the monitor and his osmotic symptoms suggest real hyperglycaemia that the HbA1c is missing.
why_wrong: A. HbA1c is only reliable when red cell survival and haemoglobin structure are normal. B. Repeating the same unreliable test will not resolve the discrepancy. C. Changing the target does not fix a measurement that is inaccurate. D. His sensor has been validated against finger-prick readings and matches his symptoms, so it is the more trustworthy measure.
pearl: Discuss a suspected haemoglobin variant with the laboratory: some HbA1c methods are affected and others are not, and the report may flag the variant.
thinking: HbA1c in range ↓ Monitor and symptoms show sustained hyperglycaemia ↓ Known haemoglobin variant ↓ HbA1c may be misleading ↓ Use alternative measures of glucose control
exam_trap: A, Accept the HbA1c — HbA1c is the usual cornerstone of monitoring, but trusting it here would leave genuine hyperglycaemia untreated.
takeaway: When HbA1c disagrees with glucose readings, especially with a haemoglobin variant, investigate and use alternative measures of glucose control.
notes: Reviewer fix: Stem/why_wrong: CGM accuracy now stated as validated against finger-prick readings (was 'meter' for a CGM user)

stem:
A 60-year-old man had a large pituitary macroadenoma removed and then received radiotherapy eight years ago. He now reports that over the past few months he has felt slow, cold and constipated and has put on weight. His free T4 is below the reference range, but his TSH is within the normal range.

What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: A low free T4 should normally drive the pituitary to produce a high TSH. A normal or low TSH alongside a low free T4 is therefore inappropriate and indicates that the pituitary is failing to stimulate the thyroid. His previous pituitary surgery and radiotherapy are classic causes of central hypothyroidism, and other pituitary hormones, especially ACTH, should be assessed before starting levothyroxine.
why_wrong: A. Primary thyroid failure would produce a raised TSH. C. Non-thyroidal illness occurs in acutely unwell patients, not in someone with gradual symptoms and a clear pituitary history. D. Subclinical hypothyroidism means a raised TSH with a normal free T4. E. Thyrotoxicosis would give a high free T4 and hyperthyroid symptoms.
pearl: In central hypothyroidism TSH cannot be used to titrate levothyroxine; the dose is adjusted to keep free T4 in the upper half of the reference range.
thinking: Hypothyroid symptoms ↓ Free T4 low ↓ TSH not raised, which is inappropriate ↓ Previous pituitary surgery and radiotherapy ↓ Central hypothyroidism
exam_trap: A, Primary hypothyroidism — the symptoms and low T4 fit, but the normal TSH is the key clue; in primary disease it would be clearly raised.
takeaway: A low free T4 with a normal or low TSH suggests pituitary or hypothalamic (central) hypothyroidism.

stem:
A 55-year-old man sees his GP because of constipation, dry skin, a hoarse voice and feeling sluggish over the winter. He takes no regular medicines and has not been unwell recently. Blood tests show a TSH well above the reference range and a free T4 below it.

Which pattern do these results represent?
why_correct: When the thyroid gland itself fails, free T4 falls and the healthy pituitary responds by increasing TSH. A high TSH with a low free T4 is therefore the pattern of primary hypothyroidism, which fits his symptoms. In the UK the commonest cause is autoimmune (Hashimoto) thyroiditis.
why_wrong: B. Pituitary failure gives a low free T4 with a low or inappropriately normal TSH. C. Subclinical hypothyroidism is a raised TSH with a normal free T4. D. Hyperthyroidism gives a suppressed TSH with a high free T4. E. Non-thyroidal illness occurs in acutely unwell patients and usually shows a low or normal TSH.
pearl: Overt primary hypothyroidism with symptoms is treated with levothyroxine, starting at a lower dose in older people or those with ischaemic heart disease.
thinking: Hypothyroid symptoms ↓ Free T4 low ↓ TSH high, so the pituitary is responding normally ↓ Fault lies in the thyroid gland ↓ Primary hypothyroidism
exam_trap: C, Subclinical hypothyroidism — it also has a raised TSH, but by definition the free T4 is normal; here it is low, making the disease overt.
takeaway: A raised TSH with a low free T4 indicates primary hypothyroidism.
